You are a single test-authoring agent. Your only goal is to write one genuine
pytest regression test for the supplied bug-fix commit. The test must fail at
the broken parent, pass at the fix, exercise behavior changed by the fix, and
avoid collateral changes.

Work empirically. First inspect nearby tests, fixtures, and parent-side source.
Stage a test, run it at the fix, and use the actual failure output to repair it.
Then run it at the parent. If it passes there, tighten the assertion so it
reproduces the reported bug. Use `check_gates` only when the staged test is a
plausible regression test; at most five gate checks are available. A passing
gate check ends the case automatically.

Use only the provided tools. `write_test` can stage one new test file; it cannot
edit repository source or existing tests. Reads and searches always inspect the
broken parent checkout. Read small windows instead of trying to reconstruct
whole files. Prefer existing public APIs and repository fixtures over mocks of
implementation details.

Do not game the transition. In particular, do not inspect source files, git
history, package versions, commit identifiers, environment markers, or the
presence of new symbols at test runtime. Do not use unconditional failures,
intentional import/collection errors, skips, xfails, timing races, or assertions
whose only purpose is to distinguish the two checkouts. The parent failure must
demonstrate the issue's externally observable behavior, and the fix pass must
demonstrate its correction. APIs used by the test must already exist at the
parent unless the issue is explicitly about a newly supported input to an
existing API.

Tool errors are written to help you recover. Follow their suggested next action.
Long tool output ends with an explicit truncation marker; narrow the query or
read another window rather than assuming omitted text is absent.

When you have a credible staged test, call `check_gates`. Do not merely describe
a test in prose. If you cannot produce a credible test within the limits, state
the blocker briefly and stop; never fabricate a passing result.

Case: pallets/flask#4420
Repository: pallets/flask
Broken parent: fdac8a5404e3e3a316568107a293f134707c75bb
Fixed commit: 17c46b2ddd8b5111369cdc68d5e0e46e9aa46ade

Linked issues:
Issue #4419:
The `flask` CLI uses `pkg_resources` (a part of `setuptools`) to detect plugin-provided subcommands, and fails silently when it's not available (see [here](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/fdac8a5404e3e3a316568107a293f134707c75bb/src/flask/cli.py#L498)). This isn't usually an issue because most environments will have pip, and therefore setuptools and pkg_resources, installed, but it does cause issues when in a hermetic environment, like Nix (see https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/155245) or a sufficiently fancy Docker container. It would be nice to make the soft dependency explicit, maybe as a setup.py extra, or even make it a hard dependency.

I'm not sure this fully qualifies as a bug, but I don't really know where else to report this, so here it is.

Pull request title:
cli: use importlib.metadata instead of pkg_resources

Now I understand the test infrastructure. The key insight is that the old code uses `pkg_resources.iter_entry_points("flask.commands")` and silently returns when `pkg_resources` is not importable. The new code uses `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="flask.commands")`.

I need to write a test that:
1. Creates a Flask CLI group
2. Registers an entry point for `flask.commands` 
3. Verifies that the plugin command is loaded

The test should fail at the parent because... wait, actually the parent code works fine when `pkg_resources` IS available. The bug is specifically about when `pkg_resources` is NOT available. Let me think about this differently.

The issue is that when `pkg_resources` is not installed, the old code silently skips loading plugin commands. The fix makes it use `importlib.metadata` instead, which is always available.

So the test should verify that plugin commands are loaded even when `pkg_resources` is not available. I can simulate this by mocking `pkg_resources` to be unavailable (raising ImportError) and then verifying that plugin commands still get loaded via `importlib.metadata`.

Wait, but at the parent, `importlib.metadata` is not used at all. The parent only uses `pkg_resources`. So if I mock `pkg_resources` to be unavailable, the parent will silently return without loading plugins. At the fix, it will use `importlib.metadata` and load plugins.

Let me think about how to create a test entry point. I can use `importlib.metadata.EntryPoint` or I can use `pkg_resources` to create one. Actually, the cleanest approach is to mock `metadata.entry_points` at the fix side... but wait, at the parent side, `metadata` doesn't exist in `flask.cli`.

Let me reconsider. The test needs to:
- At parent: fail because when `pkg_resources` is not available, plugin commands are silently skipped
- At fix: pass because `importlib.metadata` is used instead

I can mock `pkg_resources` to raise `ImportError` and then check that plugin commands are loaded. But at the parent, the code catches ImportError and returns early. At the fix, the code doesn't use `pkg_resources` at all.

Actually, let me look more carefully. At the fix, the code imports `metadata` at module level and uses `metadata.entry_points(group="flask.commands")`. At the parent, it uses `pkg_resources.iter_entry_points("flask.commands")`.

The simplest approach: mock `pkg_resources` to raise `ImportError` when imported. At the parent, this causes `_load_plugin_commands` to return early without loading plugins. At the fix, `pkg_resources` is never imported, so the mock has no effect, and `importlib.metadata` is used instead.

But wait - at the fix, the `import pkg_resources` line is removed entirely. So mocking `pkg_resources` won't affect the fix at all. The fix will use `importlib.metadata` regardless.

Let me check if `importlib.metadata` is available at the parent. It's part of Python 3.8+ standard library, so yes it's available. But the parent code doesn't use it.

Let me write a test that:
1. Uses `unittest.mock.patch` to make `pkg_resources` import raise `ImportError`
2. Creates a `FlaskGroup` with a `create_app` function
3. Registers a test entry point for `flask.commands` using `importlib.metadata` (or `pkg_resources`)
4. Invokes the CLI and checks that the plugin command is available
